summary.text:
A very clean paper on a very clean book. All external debt is PWLB and all of it is HRA. The whole book is two loans: £25m maturity at 1.63% maturing 2035, and £51.548m EIP at 3.03% maturing 2042. Reconciliation to our file ties to the pound — £76,547,733 at 2.5728% against their printed £76.548m at 2.57%.

The 2.57% weighted rate is the lowest whole-book rate we have priced this year. On the DMO's premature-repayment curve both loans are below par, giving an indicative net discount of £10.854m (14.2% of principal) — which is not a signal to break them, it is the value of the low rates they hold against a curve that is now 4.5%-5%. That £10.9m of embedded value belongs to the tenants.

Balance sheet identity ties exactly at both year-ends. 100.113 − 79.769 − 0 = 20.344, printed 20.344. 102.722 − 76.548 − 0 = 26.174, printed 26.174. The Appendix A version prints slightly different figures (20.321 and 26.152) because it uses 'gross borrowing requirement carried forward' rather than external debt in force; £22k gap is the way the £3.221m short-term slice sits inside the year, and both tables are internally consistent.

Internal borrowing has grown from £20.344m to £26.174m in the year and reserves-held investments have fallen from £62.767m to £43.141m — the council has been deliberately funding its capital programme (the New Depot in particular, §3.4 of the Q1 report) from cash rather than drawing new debt. That's how the loan book stayed flat.

Distinctive numbers: financing costs to net revenue stream are negative on both accounts — Non-HRA (8.59%) and HRA (2.35%) — because investment income exceeds interest paid. Very few authorities we have read are net investment-income positive on both. The whole £41m non-HRA authorised limit has never been used; a district that has never externally borrowed for its General Fund is rare and worth noting. The MUFG benchmark shows SK beating the district weighted average return every quarter of 25/26 (Q1 4.49% vs 4.40%, Q4 4.28% vs 4.08%), at higher weighted credit risk in Q1 and Q3.

The maturity profile is heavily concentrated in the 5-10y bucket at £41.109m (53.7%) — but that's dominated by the £25m maturity loan (9 years to run) and 5 years of EIP amortisation of the settlement loan. The only lump refinancing event on the whole book is the £25m in 2035. Nothing else needs refinancing — the EIP profile pays itself down at £3.222m/year to 2042.

Two small items to note internally: (i) the Q1 report's economic-update wording 'MUFG predict a fall to 3.75% by the end of 2026/27' is a copy-paste artefact (Bank Rate has been 3.75% since December 2025) — the two papers at the same meeting take slightly different views on the timing of the next cut but both effectively price no further move in 26/27; (ii) the CCLA Local Authority Property Fund position (£3m cost, £2.619m fair value, £0.748m lifetime dividends vs £0.381m current notional loss) is small in the context of the whole book but sits on the statutory override until 1 April 2029.

officer.subject: Your two PWLB loans at 2.57% — the same figures our file holds
officer.body:
Dear David,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Annual Report and Q1 report that went to Governance and Audit on 23 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The papers are clean and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

Starting with the loan-book reconciliation because it's the easiest cross-check. Our file for South Kesteven holds two PWLB loans totalling £76,547,733 at a weighted 2.5728%, matching your covering §3.7 print of £76.548m at 2.57%. The two loans are the £25m maturity at 1.63% (matures March 2035) and the £51.548m EIP at 3.03% (matures March 2042, £3.222m per year) — the HRA settlement pair. Together they reproduce the six-band maturity table in Appendix A at 30 June (item 51936 p.1) exactly.

What the reconciliation lets us do is price both loans daily against the DMO premature-repayment curve at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis. Both currently sit deep below par — the 1.63% is roughly £5.5m in the money and the 3.03% roughly £5.4m, an indicative net discount of about £10.9m or 14.2% of principal. Nothing to be done about that — it's the value of holding 1.63% and 3.03% money against a curve now 4.5-5% — but if members ever ask what the low rates are worth in cash terms, that is the number. Break costs from us are indicative only; only the DMO can quote.

One piece of market context. Both papers effectively price no further Bank Rate move in 26/27 — §3.23 of the Annual Report and §3.13 of the Q1 report — and the long end of the PWLB curve today is higher than it was at the 27 February 2025 strategy date, even after 75bp of Bank Rate cuts since. The live curve and SONIA path are at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard.

One standing point because CIPFA's forthcoming Prudential and Treasury Code updates will put it in front of every S151: the liability benchmark pathway is becoming central to how the whole strategy is framed. An interactive version tied to our rate feeds sits at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. For a council whose loan book runs off with no lump refinancing until March 2035, being able to move the reserves path against a live curve makes the size of that £25m event legible in a way a printed chart can't.

One feature worth naming from the papers: the ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is negative on both accounts, (8.59%) Non-HRA and (2.35%) HRA (Appendix A p.2). The General Fund has no external debt — the £41m non-HRA authorised-limit line sat fully unused all year — and investment income exceeds interest paid on both accounts. Of the councils we've read this year, being investment-income positive on both is unusual, and the MUFG benchmark shows South Kesteven beating the district weighted-average return every quarter of 25/26.

On training, three look most relevant. HRA settlement loans: EIP vs maturity mechanics sits on the shape of PW500656. Liability Benchmark: using it in practice covers what the interactive version does with the 2035 event. Capital & Treasury Strategy — for members is written for the Governance and Audit seat. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts are available for the whole team.

And if any of it is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Sources: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025/26 and Treasury Management Report Quarter 1 2026/27, Governance and Audit Committee, 23 July 2026. At https://southkesteven.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s51933/treasury-management-annual-report-2025-2026.pdf and https://southkesteven.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s51935/treasury-management-report-quarter-1-202627.pdf, with appendices at s51934 and s51936.

officer.voice: Russell Tew, first person. Not templated: no bold headers, no bulleted summary, contractions throughout. Leads with the loan-book reconciliation (ties to the pound), moves to the two loans and their embedded value against today's curve, then the smaller point about the two papers' slightly different framings of the next Bank Rate cut and the rate move from strategy date, then the standing liability-benchmark note, then the distinctive point about both financing-cost ratios being negative — as a strength named on their behalf, not a critique. No advice, no recommendation to break either loan, no invitation to correct. Break costs presented as data about value held, with the DMO disclaimer inline.
